item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Wouldn't a 10 megaton explosion (even without the radioactivity) have been noticed by a considerable number of world governments? The fireball from a nuke of that size is kilometers across, and when they detonated Ivy Mike (~10 megatons) in the Bikini Atoll, seismic activity was picked up in San Francisco.

I feel like that fourth flick test needs to be expanded upon. If it really was bigger than they expected, was their testing facility destroyed? Was mass dissemination of misinformation needed to pass off the explosion as something other than what it was? A nuclear test by the DPRK? A giant meteor strike?

I am really curious about this.

item.title: Lighter Security
item.content:encoded:
I have to disagree with you there. The Foundation has a lot of anomalous items, many of which can easily be contained by a safe. By limiting access to Foundation sites, you're already limiting access to these objects.

I think the guard thing is actually a bit overkill. Put it in a room with a bunch of safes containing other anomalous items, each marked with their contents' SCP numbers, and guard that room. Don't give any guards access to the items; don't let anyone without O5 approval go in the room, and you're as safe as those safes.

Imagine if every anomalous item in a safe required a guard; you'd have way more security personnel than an organization trying to keep itself unknown could possibly handle.

item.content:encoded:
This has been pointed out already, but

SCP-403 is to be sealed in a steel safe with a combination known only by Dr. ████ ███████.

is just preposterous. We're meant to believe that the Foundation is entrusting the safety of the whole continent planet solar system to one guy? You'd think access to this would require O5 approval, and that it would be kept in a fortified location and guarded by a lot more than 2 security personnel. Just saying.

I'm also not a fan of how the lighter was found in the cafeteria - nothing wrong with that in itself, but there should at least by an emphasis on the mystery of the lighter's origin, or some speculation as to how it got there in the first place.

Otherwise, I actually like this article, it's short and sweet. +1

item.content:encoded:
So basically, it's more powerful than a nuclear bomb, leaves behind none of the radiation a nuclear bomb would leave, and doesn't harm the user…and no one has thought of sending one person into the middle of, say, a town, and having that person ignite it three or four times? I mean, that's fortunate for the people of the world's towns, but seriously, this seems like a much better idea than a nuclear bomb. I don't condone the use of any sort of weapon of mass destruction, mind you; I'm just saying, if you must bomb someone, why not use this thing instead?
Just a thought.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
My only quibble is with the 'massive matter/antimatter explosion' bit.

While any appreciable reaction of total-annihilation matter/antimatter would count as 'massive', the wording suggests that it would equal a *whole lot* of it. A Kilogram of antimatter, if it was fully mixed with matter so that there was total annihilation of both, would basically erase half of the North American continent. There is a *lot* of energy locked away in matter.

It's just a minor…impression thing, and may only twig with me because of various science fiction stories that vastly underestimate the power of antimatter reactions. (I'm looking at you, Star Trek. Those photon torpedoes, if they really had several kilos of pre-mixed matter/antimatter, would devastate *planets*, not take shields down to 60%)
